text:
The question of possible accretion at the base of ice shelves is of great interest to oceanographers as well as glaciologists. The mechanisms for transfer or removal of the latent heat of freezing are not clear, and on a theoretical basis, significant sea-ice accretion would not seem possible unless the latent heat is removed by the water rather than the ice.
The relationship of the ice shelf and its underlying water to the general oceanography of the open ocean is of interest. To attack this question we must have some information regarding 1) the type and magnitude of the interaction between the shelf ice and underlying water, and 2) the heat and salt flux across the boundary between the Ross Sea and the sub-Ross Ice Shelf waters. Oceanographic and ice-core data from a locality where accretion is suspected, combined with concurrent measurements in front of the Ross Barrier, will be necessary.
The unique boundary conditions of the water beneath the ice shelf are significant. Thermohaline-induced convection and microstructure may produce a circulation pattern without interference from the wind. An opportunity to measure in nature a purely thermohaline-induced convection pattern, which can be related to laboratory models, is thus present. The detailed tidal measurements suggested as part of the geophysical program will be of great value in these studies.
Within the water column below the RISP hole, standard oceanographic measurements of temperature, salinity, dissolved gases, nutrient concentrations, stable isotopes (deuterium and 0-18), decay isotopes (C-14 and tritium), currents (all three components of the velocity field), suspended material, and bottom photographs will be made.
